(1) part-time work and full-time education are complementary rather than substitutable, and (2) the part-time work experience of teenagers in fulltime education is a positive influence on the transition to full-time work.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the extent of part-time work among full-time school students; how this varies by school subject and school type, as well as by gender and age; the relationship between part-time work and educational attainment; and the impact of part-time work on educational attainment, as well as the impact of educational attainment on part-time work.
the labour supply of teenagers, and with the implications of this labour supply for educational decisions and policy, and for the labour market outcomes of young people in the longer run.
the labour supply decisions of teenagers in full time education.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the labour force participation of teenagers in full- time education has been largely overlooked in analyses of the youth labour market and in analyses of educational decisions and policies.

the labour supply of teenagers is not a single transition from full-time education into work, but rather a complex set of overlapping transitions, which include part-time work in education as well as the school-leaving transition.
part-time work and education are not incompatible.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
part-time jobs are a significant part of teenage labour supply, and that the part-time employment of teenagers has increased in recent years.
the part-time employment of teenagers in full time education has been neglected, but is a significant phenomenon which deserves further study.
part-time work is an important part of the labour market experience of many young people in full-time education, but that there is considerable variation in the extent to which this is the case.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a strong positive relationship between part-time work and academic performance.
there are a number of factors that influence the decision to take up a part-time job while studying, and that the decision to work is not made in isolation from the decision to stay in education.
there is no single ‘school leaving’ decision.
